Inspired by Calen's recent wild pics and Rick's colorful division, I took some more photos of the collection. AFter 2 hours of trying to upload some pix, I wasn't able to get them all, but here's most of them. Photos taken 7/13/15.


Here's the population overview, look at all those different colors and subtle variations in shape:




Seems like this clone has an extreme red throat flipped up onto the top of the lid:



Mug shot:



More on the red side:



The color on the "body" seems to have faded on this clone, yet the interior became even more colorful. How cool is that?! Lots of phenotypic variation-this clone was darker red earlier this year.



Some amazing shapes:



A beautiful deep red clone:



And another nice red clone:



Some of the lids stay nice and green even though they've aged a bit. Typically, the entire trap, including the lid, becomes darker red over time. I bet this is environmental, and the lid under a different grow environment could turn reddish as it ages:






In contrast, and much like the liberty County, FL rubricorporas, many of the lids turn solid red over time. This clone pictured below is very peculiar in the sense that it has a yellow edging around the lid. I think it's highly environmentally induced:



Crappy shot, but check out the amazing shape of this lid, as well as the intricate venation:





Last but not least, an incredible dark red clone:



Closer shot of this dark clone:

posts.body_html:
Gorgeous! Love the diversity - I'll take a mixed bag like this over a uniformly solid red population any day.

Very curious to see if these guys turn solid red by late summer outdoors in Cali. One thought that has occurred to me is that the frequent overcast days in the FL summer act much like polycarb in a greenhouse, which diffuses the light and (somewhat counter-intuitively) brings out more extreme red colors. This is the well-known polycarb "fake tan" effect lol but I SUSPECT that light diffusion due to cloud layer may play a significant role in the way wild Sarrs color. We are fortunate to get mostly cloudless summer and fall days in Cali and if natural light diffusion does play a role, I would expect less coloration in CA even in full sun.

posts.body_html:
Really happy with my Bay Co. rubricorporas this season. Up until 2017 I had multiple divisions crammed into 5.5" pots - not ideal for getting big mature plants. This year they are still showing the effects of that size-wise - next year I predict monsters - but the color is by far the best I've gotten so far. I grow 4 or 5 clones and most of them came up "actual red tube" this season rather than ornata. Seems like color can vary a lot on these depending on environmental conditions. When meizzwang visited the wild site in 2013 every plant was solid red, but when DirtyDivisions and I went in fall 2016 it was a much more mixed bag. Let's go to the tape!
I have all my plants spaced out into a cement mixing tub (idea stolen from Mike of course) where they should be able to grow extensive roots and get big:

Hard to tell from the pic but this clone has a crazy mouth and lid, and solid red color this year:

Smaller pitchers on the same clone, pic from last week - look at that color and shape

You can see the color progression with time from the unopened trap on the left, to the 3 day old trap in the middle, to the 10 day old trap on the right. If you look carefully you'll see a SUPER red plant right behind this one. Unfortunately it's also SUPER slow growing.

Interestingly, these rubricorporas from Bay Co, FL will likely be the first to bloom this year! Pics taken 2/24/20:




Every year, a different clone blooms first, indicating that environment likely plays a bigger role in the speed of development rather than genetics. This was the first to bloom a few years back, this is S. flava 'heavy veins' which is a few days behind the rubricorporas this year :

Totally forgot to update this thread! So, in case I haven't already said it, this population is consistently the tallest out of all the flava populations that I grow! Other can get taller, but these are really tall year after year! Here's a pic from last year, a giant rugelii trap compared to a regular, tall rubricorpora Bay Co, FL trap!


Here are some updated pics, mostly taken early June 2022. Several clones colored up even before they opened up, which is unusual for this population in particular. They ususally turn red as the traps age:














Notice how all the phyllodia was left on from the previous years' growth:
